{"id": "12:16/q18", "question": "How can recoverable omission and oblique expression serve the passage's style?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:16/q18/p1", "position": "A recoverable object can be omitted for graceful, balanced, deliberately indirect speech.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī illustrates object omission with 'two women watering' in 28:23, where their camels are understood, and with poetry. {"id": "12:16/q20", "question": "What effect does the imperfect yabkūn have after the past verb wajāʾū?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:16/q20/p1", "position": "It makes the past scene vivid as a present state, with the brothers' weeping underway at arrival and continually renewed.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says the present verb in the circumstantial phrase depicts action ongoing at arrival and renewed moment by moment. Al-Itqān calls the imperfect after a past event narration of a past scene as present, showing its state then and its ongoing renewal."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q01", "question": "What happened when the brothers brought this story to Jacob?", "turns_on": "The reports give different amounts of dialogue and different accounts of Jacob's physical reaction.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q01/p1", "position": "They returned at night, feigning grief, and told Jacob they had raced, left Joseph with their things, and lost him to a wolf.", "reasons": "Muqatil places their return at the evening prayer and calls the outing hunting; Ibn Kathir says they had already put Joseph in the well. Qurtubi says darkness made their excuse easier and cites a saying about favors at night and excuses for daytime wrongs. Bursevi says Jacob asked after them, their sheep, and Joseph, and they said the matter was worse."}, {"id": "12:17/q01/p2", "position": "Jacob asked what had happened and where Joseph was, heard the wolf story, cried out, and asked for Joseph's shirt.", "reasons": "Thalabi's al-Suddi says Jacob first feared harm to the brothers or sheep; Study Quran's Bg says they told him the sheep were safe before his question. Qurtubi gives the dialogue and his request for the shirt."}, {"id": "12:17/q01/p3", "position": "Jacob fainted at the news and did not revive until dawn.", "reasons": "Qurtubi's al-Suddi and Ibn Hibban report Judah found no sign of life, lamented losing brother and father, and Reuben supported Jacob on waking; Wahb reports Judah checking breath and pulse and rebuking the brothers. Study Quran's Q adds that they poured water on Jacob."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q02", "question": "What did the brothers mean by نَسْتَبِقُ?", "turns_on": "The text names no equipment or venue; the attributed shooting reading, reports, word form, and practical purpose supply the proposed details.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q02/p1", "position": "They raced one another on foot to see who was fastest.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Jubba'i and others are cited; Wahidi and Razi answer the objection that adult running is childish by its use in war and protecting flocks, as do Qushayri and Alusi. Tabatabai locates it in open country; Study Quran's R says wolves had taken sheep. Islahi cites the race to the door at 12:25."}, {"id": "12:17/q02/p2", "position": "They competed in archery or shooting.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba notes sabq can mean a prize; Mawradi derives the form from sabāq. Thalabi, Wahidi, Tabarsi, Qurtubi, and Alusi cite a reading ascribed to ʿAbd Allah, with forms recorded as nantaḍil, nantaṣil, or nintadil, meaning shooting. Wahidi and Razi cite the Prophetic prize rule and comparison of arrow distance. Alusi favors archery on the reading's evidence; Qurtubi reports Azhari's distinction between arrow contests and horse races. Damghani includes shooting and competing in archery among the senses of istibaq."}, {"id": "12:17/q02/p3", "position": "They went hunting or competed to catch game.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls the outing hunting; Mawradi offers catching game as one possible contest, as do Ibn Jawzi, Abu Hayyan, and Alusi. Damghani also gives hunting as a sense of istibaq."}, {"id": "12:17/q02/p4", "position": "They competed at practical work, including watering, herding, or gathering wood.", "reasons": "Mawradi proposes their work; Abu Hayyan and Alusi mention divided farm or flock tasks."}, {"id": "12:17/q02/p5", "position": "They could have raced on horseback.", "reasons": "Abu Nasr al-Qushayri lists horseback competition alongside archery and running."}, {"id": "12:17/q02/p6", "position": "The form means striving for precedence in a mutual race; iftiʿāl and tafāʿul can overlap.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Samin, Alusi, and Zamakhshari as quoted by Tabatabai compare the derived forms; Raghib defines sabq as preceding in movement. Tabatabai says each agent's self-directed effort entails comparison, citing good deeds and the door race against al-Manar's proposed distinction. Jishumi calls istibaq racing to get ahead."}, {"id": "12:17/q02/p7", "position": "Istibāq specifically means trying to get ahead, in distinction from reciprocal racing.", "reasons": "Al-Manar applies the distinction here and contrasts racing to good deeds and to the door; Tabatabai rejects it because those examples also involve striving to get ahead."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q03", "question": "What does the verse imply about the legitimacy and purpose of racing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q03/p1", "position": "Racing and archery are legitimate practices, especially as training for war or defense.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports permissibility of foot racing and wrestling while noting debate over payment and binding contracts. Tabarsi says archery is permitted by consensus and horse and camel races by his school. Ibn al-ʿArabi cites the Prophet's foot and horse races and his two races with Aisha; Qurtubi cites Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ's race reported by Muslim, the Prophet's horse races in Malik from al-Hafya and Thaniyyat al-Wadaʿ, and travelers' archery in Muslim. Bukhari's al-ʿAdba report adds the Prophet's lesson that God lowers worldly things that rise."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q04", "question": "Which contests may carry a prize or wager?", "turns_on": "The disagreement concerns the scope of the prize hadith, military benefit, and whether a paid contest becomes gambling.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q04/p1", "position": "Prizes are confined to archery, camel racing, and horse racing.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites consensus, Abu Hurayra's hadith in al-Nasa'i, and reliance by Hijazi and Iraqi jurists; Shafiʿi calls wagering elsewhere gambling. Wahidi and Razi cite the same threefold Prophetic rule. The purported addition 'or wing' was, Qurtubi says, fabricated by Abu al-Bakhtari for al-Rashid and scholars rejected his reports."}, {"id": "12:17/q04/p2", "position": "Only horses and archery may carry prizes, with horse racing preferable.", "reasons": "Malik grounds the restriction in military usefulness; Qurtubi observes that the hadith's wording also includes camels."}, {"id": "12:17/q04/p3", "position": "Only horse racing may carry a wager.", "reasons": "Qurtubi attributes this to jurists who treat horse racing as the customary Arab race."}, {"id": "12:17/q04/p4", "position": "Any contest may carry a wager.", "reasons": "Qurtubi attributes this to ʿAtaʾ but argues it would permit gambling, which is agreed to be forbidden."}, {"id": "12:17/q04/p5", "position": "Foot racing and wrestling with prizes are forbidden.", "reasons": "Tabarsi attributes this to his school and al-Shafiʿi; Jishumi also notes disagreement over compensation."}, {"id": "12:17/q04/p6", "

{"id": "12:17/q05", "question": "What stake arrangements are permitted in a race?", "turns_on": "Whether the third entrant has a real chance to win and thereby prevents a two-person stake from being gambling.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q05/p1", "position": "A voluntary known prize from a donor or a one-sided stake is allowed.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says neither arrangement is disputed; the winner may take the one-sided stake and the loser cannot reclaim it."}, {"id": "12:17/q05/p2", "position": "Two-sided stakes require a genuine third contestant who could win without risking money.", "reasons": "Qurtubi describes how either racer or the third entrant receives both stakes if victorious; Abu Ali ibn Khayran says the entrant's ability must be uncertain, whence muhallil. A Prophetic report and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib support the qualifying horse, as do Shafiʿi and most scholars. Malik first dispensed with it but later required it, a view Qurtubi calls better. Without one, Qurtubi reports consensus that the wager is forbidden gambling."}, {"id": "12:17/q05/p3", "position": "A qualifying third entrant is unnecessary for two-sided stakes.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Malik's earlier view; Malik later changed it and Qurtubi favors his later requirement."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q06", "question": "What makes a race or archery contest properly specified?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q06/p1", "position": "The course, competitors, and victory criterion must be specified appropriately.", "reasons": "Qurtubi derives from Malik's report a known distance, comparable horses, and separate distances for trained and untrained horses; he reserves the military Sunnah for horses prepared against enemies, not civil conflict. He also requires a known finish for camels, and a target, round count, and hit criterion for archery. He reports Umar's preference that the owner ride, while Qurtubi requires an adult rider; Shafiʿi and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan measure a lead by muzzle or hindquarters, also for archers. In a report of the Prophet racing Abu Bakr and Umar, Abu Bakr's second place means his horse's head reached the Prophet's horse's rear."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q07", "question": "What is the brothers' مَتَٰعِنَا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q07/p1", "position": "Their clothes and other belongings or baggage.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says clothes and belongings; Baghawi, Ibn Jawzi, Abu Hayyan, Qurtubi, and Study Quran's Bg emphasize garments. Abu Hayyan says they took off their clothes while competing and sees this as evidence Joseph was young rather than adolescent. Bursevi includes provisions and notes matāʿ means food containers at 12:65."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q08", "question": "Why did they say they left Joseph by the belongings?", "turns_on": "The narrative leaves their stated reason for leaving him implicit; sources infer it from his placement among their things.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q08/p1", "position": "They present Joseph as guarding the baggage.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabarsi make him the watcher; Qurtubi also says he guarded clothes and other belongings. Mawradi says this may have been their reason for leaving him."}, {"id": "12:17/q08/p2", "position": "They present the place as safe, showing care for Joseph and denying neglect.", "reasons": "Mawradi proposes concern for him. Alusi says clothes and provisions kept him within sight, briefly alone, unlikely to face danger; he also quotes Shaykh al-Islam on the safe setting."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q09", "question": "What did they claim the wolf had eaten?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun and plain wording refer to Joseph or allow a displaced reference to the baggage.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q09/p1", "position": "They claimed the wolf killed Joseph and ate him, or some of him.", "reasons": "Razi favors this reading; Alusi calls it the plain sense. Ibn Ashur says 'ate him' can designate a whole person while meaning some of him, citing 5:3 and a lion example; he takes the singular wolf collectively as a pack leaving no trace, which explains the absence of burial. Bursevi says their sequence depicts an immediate attack after leaving him. Khattabi says their claim was that the wolf consumed Joseph entirely, leaving no trace and preempting a demand for surviving evidence. Samarrai contrasts eating with merely preying on him, which would have torn his shirt."}, {"id": "12:17/q09/p2", "position": "They may have meant that the wolf attacked the belongings rather than Joseph.", "reasons": "Razi records the proposal that the brothers exposed the baggage to a wolf but prefers the first interpretation; Alusi rejects the proposal as departing from the plain wording."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q10", "question": "Why did the brothers choose a wolf for their story?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q10/p1", "position": "They reused Jacob's earlier stated fear of a wolf, though the excuse was weak and exposed their deception.", "reasons": "Mawradi, Qurtubi, and Islahi say they borrowed his own warning; Ibn Kathir calls the admission of likely disbelief calculated tact, since the coincidence sounds unlikely. Islahi calls it unintelligent; Biqai cites their suspicious behavior and telltale signs, despite no prior proven lie."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q11", "question": "How is ٱلذِّئْبُ read?", "turns_on": "Whether to realize or soften the hamza, including the analogy Kisai raises with the fish wording.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q11/p1", "position": "The hamza is articulated: al-dhiʾbu.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni reports Hamza ibn Habib's reading against Kisai's; Tabarsi attributes articulation to readers other than his listed softeners. Qiraat ER calls it the standard connected reading; in pause the final consonant becomes silent. Kisai asks why Hamza hamzates wolf but not the fish at 37:142; the excerpt gives no reply. Ibn Jinni notes that early reading arguments began with analogy of forms or roots and later added grammar and citations."}, {"id": "12:17/q11/p2", "position": "The hamza is softened or dropped, yielding al-dhību.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni reports Kisai's unhamzated form; Tabarsi lists Kisai, Khalaf, Abu Jafar, Warsh, al-Asha, and al-Yazidi in all three occurrences. Qiraat ER describes compensatory lengthening. Tabarsi also gives plurals adhuʾub, dhawāʾib, and dhuʾbān and the wind verb tadhāʾabat."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q12", "question": "What does مُؤْمِنٍۢ لَّنَا mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q12/p1", "position": "Someone who believes, credits, or accepts their account.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba derives iman from affirmation and cites ordinary speech, 40:12, and prayer called iman at 2:143; Bursevi distinguishes verbal declaration of a speaker's truth from inward acceptance and defines truth against falsehood. Tabatabai notes the verb takes li or bi, citing 29:26; Ibn Ashur cites 29:26 and 10:83 for li before a person. Wahidi points to discussion at 2:3. Tabari's al-Suddi glosses it this way, while Tabari rejects reading the brothers as confessing lies or accusing Jacob of disbelief in known truth. Ibn Jawzi's Nuzha reports a Qur'anic sense of assent or believing something true, mentioning 40:12."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q13", "question": "What other senses and theological uses of īmān and al-Muʾmin are brought to bear?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine name is explained through affirmation or the granting of safety.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q13/p1", "position": "A human believer affirms; God is al-Muʾmin by confirming His promise or accepting a servant's faith.", "reasons": "Both Ibn Qutayba works give this distinction. Gharib further warns that the divine attribute cannot be conjugated at will but must follow a transmitted form from Prophet or imams. Ibn Jawzi's Nuzha cites Ibn Qutayba's gloss of God's name al-Mu'min as confirming His promise, mentioning 59:23."}, {"id": "12:17/q13/p2", "position": "The divine name al-Muʾmin may derive from granting security: none is safe unless God makes them safe.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba offers this alternative etymology alongside confirmation."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q14", "question": "Why say مُؤْمِنٍۢ rather than مُصَدِّق?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q14/p1", "position": "Muʾmin combines believing with giving security or reassurance, outweighing muṣaddiq's verbal echo of ṣādiqīn.", "reasons": "Burhan says the added security sense better suits their request. Itqan says meaning takes priority over sound embellishment and the verse keeps muʾmin despite the available rhyme."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q15", "question": "Why did they expect Jacob not to believe them?", "turns_on": "The sources point to prior distrust, absence or contradiction of evidence, and the rhetorical use of an anticipated refusal; these reasons can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q15/p1", "position": "His love for Joseph and prior suspicion of the brothers would make this particular account unbelievable to him.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says a prophet cannot reject known truth. Tabari says Jacob suspects them, not that they confess lying or accuse him of rejecting truthful people. Wahidi, Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi, and others emphasize love and distrust; Tabarsi adds jealousy and resentment. Ibn Kathir says they acknowledged his earlier warning. Study Quran links his suspicion to 12:11–12 and notes Genesis instead says he believed them. Asad says envy led him to infer harm but 12:83 shows he was unsure Joseph had died."}, {"id": "12:17/q15/p2", "position": "They provided no convincing evidence, and the available signs worked against their claim.", "reasons": "Wahidi's Abu Bakr says objective truth alone would not secure belief without signs; Baghawi likewise says no evidence was offere

Islahi calls the story weak."}, {"id": "12:17/q15/p3", "position": "Their claim of expected disbelief is a rhetorical excuse that signals their asserted truth or their expectation of rejection.", "reasons": "Tabatabai calls it a formula used when means are exhausted, indirectly claiming truth; Ibn Ashur says it shows they were not seeking credence. Biqai says they conceded Jacob's disbelief; Burhan says even manifest innocence would not sway a father favoring Joseph, but their contrived proof betrayed them."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q16", "question": "What is the force of وَلَوْ كُنَّا صَٰدِقِينَ?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣādiqīn describes their present claim, their general reputation, or a concessive assertion within their lie.", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q16/p1", "position": "Even if the brothers were normally known as honest, Jacob would doubt them about Joseph.", "reasons": "Mawradi attributes this to Ibn Jarir; Ibn Jawzi and Qurtubi attribute it to Zajjaj, Tabari, and others. Ibn Atiyya says Jacob might have believed them before this disaster but not amid grief and old suspicion, while finding al-Rummani's analogy unsound. Alusi says this avoids their admitting a lie by contrast; Bursevi allows that Jacob regards them as truthful."}, {"id": "12:17/q16/p2", "position": "Even if their present account were in fact true, Jacob would not believe it.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq is cited by Mawradi and Ibn Jawzi; Abu Bakr in Wahidi says they may believe themselves truthful but need proof. Baghawi says they could be truthful before God yet lack evidence. Abu Hayyan says the clause may limit the truth claim to this incident; Ibn Atiyya says it continues their lie."}, {"id": "12:17/q16/p3", "position": "They are asserting 'although we have told the truth' as part of the invented story.", "reasons": "Mawradi cites Ibn Ishaq's wording; Ibn Atiyya reports Mubarrad's continuation of their assertion and questions an analogy to 7:88 and al-Rummani's account. Qurtubi notes the readings 'even if' and 'even though'. Tabatabai says the excuse indirectly asserts truth. Alusi resists making it a direct confession of actual truth, since contrast would imply they were lying. Burhan observes that the brothers' wording need not concede that they were actually lying, against an inference that law necessarily makes the condition impossible."}, {"id": "12:17/q16/p4", "position": "Even if Jacob counted them truthful, he still would not believe this report.", "reasons": "Burhan reports al-Zamakhshari's account of the supposition from the addressee's perspective: even if they were reckoned truthful by Jacob."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q17", "question": "How does the concessive construction وَلَوْ كُنَّا work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q17/p1", "position": "It is an elliptical concessive or circumstantial clause: Jacob would still not believe them, even under that condition.", "reasons": "Nahhas paraphrases it with wa-in kunna; Tabarsi supplies the omitted result. Samin calls it a circumstantial clause. Ibn Ashur identifies the waw as circumstantial and law as the remotest possible condition; he says no deleted opposite condition or contrary conclusion is implied, unlike a restrictive conditional, and cites Maʿarri's verse and 2:170 and 3:91. Burhan observes that law and lammā take past-form verbs as exceptions to the usual future orientation of condition verbs. Abu al-Abbas, reported by Burhan, says law originally connects one event to another and can extend to the concessive meaning of in. Burhan reports that reading as one answer to the objection that law would imply the brothers admitted a lie; it also places this past-form conditional among examples with prospective meaning."}, {"id": "12:17/q17/p2", "position": "The hypothetical truthfulness can be framed from Jacob's perspective: even if he counted them truthful.", "reasons": "Burhan reports al-Zamakhshari's alternative to taking law as in: the condition supposes how the addressee would reckon the brothers, without making them confess a lie."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q18", "question": "How are نَسْتَبِقُ and وَتَرَكْنَا related syntactically to ذَهَبْنَا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q18/p1", "position": "Nastabiq is circumstantial, and taraknā is another circumstantial clause, with qad understood by some grammarians.", "reasons": "Samin al-Durr gives both analyses and notes the optional implicit qad."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q19", "question": "What is the grammatical role of بِـ in بِمُؤْمِنٍۢ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q19/p1", "position": "It precedes the predicate in a negative clause, a recurrent Quranic construction.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati lists this verse alongside 2:167, 11:29, 26:114, 11:83, 16:46, 40:56, 14:22, 6:134, 12:44, 12:103, 26:137–138, 27:81, 30:53, 35:22, 37:162, 52:29, and 68:2."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q20", "question": "How do the plural pronominal endings in the verse mark their speakers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q20/p1", "position": "Plural and dual suffixes use following letters for number and gender rather than the singular vowel alone.", "reasons": "Sibawayh says masculine dual and plural suffixes add mim after alif or waw; -tumā and -tumū retain ḍamma on taʾ and kaf because following material marks number and gender, and no marker beyond dual is added since dual already counts as plural. Feminine plural verb endings avoid a doubled nun unlike -tun or -kunna, to prevent four or five successive vowels."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q21", "question": "When can a hearer ask for identification after hearing a plural reference?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q21/p1", "position": "A definite named person cannot be queried as though unidentified, but an unfamiliar plural group can be.", "reasons": "Sibawayh says asking man after a specifically named Abd Allah is inappropriate; one may instead ask who he is or which man. He reports Arabs asking maʿa manīn after 'we went with them' or mannā after 'I saw him' when the people are not personally known, treating the report like 'I saw a man'."}]}
{"id": "12:17/q22", "question": "What did the brothers' shirt evidence show about the wolf story?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:17/q22/p1", "position": "They bloodied Joseph's shirt to substantiate the story, but its intact condition disclosed the lie.", "reasons": "Razi says they used a kid's blood; al-Qadi suggests they stripped Joseph before the well to prepare the ruse and says a torn shirt would have made it credible. Razi explains the next verse's 'came with his shirt with blood' as blood covering it. Farra, Mubarrad, Zajjaj, and Ibn al-Anbari read dam kadhib as blood they lied about, a verbal noun for object or agent, comparing 67:30, 68:6, 34:7. Shaʿbi says Joseph's whole story is in his shirt: bloodied here, examined for direction of tearing at 12:26, and later restoring Jacob's sight. Samarrai reasons that an actual predator's attack would have torn Joseph's clothes, whereas the shirt they displayed had false blood without such tearing, citing 12:18."}]}
